idiom_name: static array of function pointers indexed by opcode (+ bounds check)
implementation_notes: C has no table abstraction, so the classic structure is written by hand: a file-scope array of function pointers - `static int (* const table[])(struct vm *, uint8_t)` - pinned to opcodes with designated initialisers (`[OP_ADD] = do_add`), plus its element count kept next to it for the bounds check, and `table[op](vm, arg)` as the dispatch step. What replaces the classic structure is nothing but your own declaration plus the indirect call; for sparse or string keys you must add a lookup loop (linear scan or your own hash) or switch to a table of `struct { const char *name; int (*fn)(...); }`. The classic indexed form is exactly right when the key space is a small dense integer range, because it is the fastest and simplest dispatch C can express; it becomes the wrong tool as soon as keys are sparse, textual or arrive at runtime.
pitfalls: An out-of-range or unmapped opcode must be checked before the call: indexing past the array or calling through a NULL slot is undefined behaviour, not an exception.
The array decays to a pointer and loses its element count - keep the count (sizeof macro, explicit constant or a sentinel entry) beside the table so the bounds check cannot drift.
Every entry must have the exact function-pointer type; a mismatched signature survives a cast and becomes undefined behaviour at the call site.
File-scope tables are writable unless declared const (and static): without const the dispatch table can be patched at runtime, which is a bug factory and an attack surface.
